Austere

/aw-STEER/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Austere means very bare, plain, and without comfort or luxury — sometimes describing a strict, self-denying way of living.

The monastery cell was austere: stone walls, a narrow cot, and a single candle.

Worked Example

The judge was known for her austere chambers: gray walls, one lamp, and not a single photograph or plant.

Austere fits because the office is stripped down to the bare essentials — no decoration, no comfort, nothing beyond what is strictly needed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

spartan: Spartan describes rooms, gear, and lifestyles stripped to the bare essentials, with a nod to toughness — a spartan bunkroom, a spartan training camp. Austere covers the same bareness but adds a colder, more forbidding edge, and it can also describe strict self-denial. Spartan feels practical; austere can feel forbidding.

stark: Stark means harshly bare in a way that jumps out at you, and it especially describes blunt, unsoftened clarity — a stark outline, a stark contrast, a stark choice or warning. Austere describes bare places and strict living; stark describes how brutally plain and clear-cut something appears.

severe: Severe means strict and unsparing, without softness — a severe teacher, a severe haircut, severe rules. Austere leans toward bareness and lack of comfort in places and lifestyles, while severe leans toward sternness in people, style, and discipline. An austere room lacks comfort; a severe one glares at you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lavish: rich, generous, full of luxury

opulent: luxurious and richly decorated

Where it sits · how deliberately comfort is stripped away — plain → austere → ascetic

plain vs. austere: A plain room simply lacks decoration; an austere one feels deliberately stripped down to the bare minimum.

ascetic vs. austere: Austere describes severe plainness; ascetic goes even further, describing a life that rejects all comfort and pleasure as a discipline.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — austere

Root — austere: from Greek austeros, 'dry, harsh, bitter' (from auein, 'to dry') — a dried-out harshness that came to mean severe plainness

Put it together

Put it together: Austere came into English through Latin from the Greek austeros, which described a dry, bitter harshness — like an unripe fruit. Over time that 'harsh dryness' became the severe, stripped-bare plainness the word describes today.

Use the root in a new word: austerity

Use the root in a new word: austerity: After the flood wiped out its budget, the town entered a period of austerity, cutting spending on everything but the essentials.

Word Building

Word Choice

Formal / literary

Austere has two closely related faces: it describes bare, bleak places and things (an austere room, an austere landscape) and also strict, self-denying people or lifestyles (an austere monk, an austere routine). Depending on context it can sound admiring — disciplined, uncluttered — or forbidding and cold.
